title: Hydrolysis of salts
competency: Predict whether a salt solution is acidic, basic or neutral and explain why.

keywords.def: Reaction of the cation or anion of a salt with water, giving H₃O⁺ or OH⁻.
The cation of a salt gives H⁺ to water, making H₃O⁺ (acidic).
The anion of a salt takes H⁺ from water, making OH⁻ (basic).

en.text: In salt hydrolysis an ion of the salt reacts with water. Salts of a strong acid and a strong base (NaCl) do not hydrolyze: neutral. Salts of a weak acid and a strong base (CH₃COONa, Na₂CO₃) are basic, because the anion takes H⁺ from water. Salts of a strong acid and a weak base (NH₄Cl) are acidic, because the cation gives H⁺ to water.

ideas.name: Salts of a weak acid and a weak base

en.text: When both parents are weak, both ions hydrolyze. Compare Ka of the cation with Kb of the anion: if Ka > Kb the solution is acidic, if Ka < Kb it is basic, and if they are equal it is neutral. Ammonium formate is slightly acidic because Ka(NH₄⁺) = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ is larger than Kb(HCOO⁻) = 5.9 × 10⁻¹¹.

notes.text: p.40: "This conjugate acid is a strong acid" (NH₄⁺) is wrong; NH₄⁺ is a weak acid (Ka = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰). Acetate is a weak base, not "moderately strong".
Hydrolysis equations on p.40–41 use one-way arrows and H₂O(aq); they are equilibria with H₂O(l).
Activity 1.9: Kb = 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ is for cyanide CN⁻, not thiocyanate CNS⁻ (a negligible base). The lesson uses NH₄CN.
